name: The Soviet Union under Stalin
title: Social Hierarchy of Stalin's Soviet Union: From Party Elite to Gulag

tiers.name: The general secretary
tiers.you: You lead the party from Moscow; your decrees send peasants into exile and prisoners into the camps, and every key appointment in the country passes through the lists your apparatus keeps.
tiers.kid: Joseph Stalin led the Communist Party and ruled the Soviet Union; his orders sent millions of people to prison camps.
tiers.rise: Stalin reached the top through the party’s apparatus, by controlling its appointments. In 1922 Lenin allied with Leon Trotsky against the party’s growing bureaucracy and Stalin’s influence, but after Lenin’s death Stalin took control.
tiers.why: Joseph Stalin, the first general secretary of the Communist Party, ruled through the Politburo and the party apparatus he had built.

tiers.name: The nomenklatura
tiers.term: osnovnoi spisok (basic list), uchyotny spisok (registration list)
tiers.you: Your name is on the party committee’s list, and with its approval you run a factory, a farm district or a department of a ministry; your post depends on the party that gave it.
tiers.kid: Party officials ran the factories, farms, schools and offices, and the Communist Party chose every one of them.
tiers.rise: No one was born into it: a party member entered by being placed on a committee’s list and appointed to a post. Richard Pipes argued that the system continued the tsarist regime, as many former tsarist officials and careerists joined the Bolshevik government.
tiers.why: The nomenklatura were the people who held, or were listed as fit to hold, the key posts in government, industry, agriculture and education, posts filled only with the party’s approval.

tiers.name: Workers and townspeople
tiers.you: Your passport is stamped with a propiska that gives you the right to your room in the town, and a labour book records your discipline at work; miss work and you may be sentenced to forced labour.
tiers.kid: Workers in the towns carried passports that said where they were allowed to live.
tiers.rise: A peasant could settle in a town only with a passport, which peasants could obtain only by special application; the towns’ growth stopped once the restrictions began.
tiers.why: The party counted the working class as its social base, and millions moved through the country to train, take new jobs or escape repression as supposed kulaks.

tiers.name: Collective farmers
tiers.you: You work the collective farm’s fields for labour days paid in grain, keep a plot of about an acre for yourself, and cannot leave the farm or move to a town without a passport you must apply for.
tiers.kid: Farmers had to join big collective farms run by the state, and they were not free to leave them.
tiers.rise: Members had no right of free exit, and the passport that a move to town required was given to peasants only on special application; a capable member could become a brigade leader (brigadir), usually a local man.
tiers.why: Collectivization made the peasants members of collective farms (kolkhozy).

tiers.name: The disenfranchised
tiers.you: You kept a shop of your own, so you have lost the vote and may not hold a post, study at an institute or join a collective farm; to win your rights back you must prove your productive labour and your loyalty.
tiers.kid: People the government called its enemies, such as priests and private traders, lost the right to vote, to study and to join a farm.
tiers.rise: Local election commissions could restore a lishenets’s rights on proof of productive labour and loyalty to the Soviets; the Central Election Commission and the Presidium of the Central Executive Committee had the final word.
tiers.why: The constitutions of 1918 and 1924 deprived whole categories of people of the right to vote or to be elected: those who hired labour for profit or lived on unearned income, private merchants and brokers, monks and…

tiers.name: Deported peasants
tiers.you: You were labelled a kulak for owning a couple of cows more than your neighbours; your farm was seized and you were deported with your family to a settlement in the north Urals, to live on starvation rations.
tiers.kid: The government called better-off farmers its enemies, took their farms and sent many far away to cold, hungry settlements.
tiers.rise: The OGPU told the deported that they would regain their rights in five years. Former kulaks and their families went on to make up the majority of the victims of the Great Purge of the late 1930s, with 669,929 people arrested and 376,202 executed.
tiers.why: In Marxist–Leninist theory the kulaks, the better-off peasants, were class enemies of the poor.

tiers.name: Prisoners of the Gulag
tiers.you: You were sentenced under Article 58 by a troika, without a trial, and sent to a timber camp in the far north, where your food depends on how much you cut.
tiers.kid: Millions of people were sent to the Gulag, prison camps in cold, faraway places, where they were forced to work very hard.
tiers.rise: Between 1934 and 1953, 20 to 40 per cent of the prisoners were released each year, and good workers could earn early release; Naftaly Frenkel himself went from inmate to camp commander. On release many political prisoners were barred from the big cities and sent into exile in remote regions.
tiers.why: The Gulag, the Main Directorate of Correctional Labour Camps, was set up under the OGPU in 1930 and run by the NKVD from 1934.
